executive_summary.headline: Token economics become the dominant engineering problem: three independent tools shipped this week (Semble, CodeGraph v0.8.0, rtk) that each cut the token cost of a single coding-agent session by 60–98%, with reproducible benchmarks attached
executive_summary.body: The week of May 18 produced a cluster of tools aimed at making agent sessions cheaper, not smarter. Semble (MinishLab/semble, 3.6k stars, HN front page May 18: 270 pts / 89 comments) is an MIT-licensed MCP server that replaces grep+read with local semantic code retrieval, achieving 98% fewer tokens and 94% recall at 2k tokens — where grep+read needs a 100k context window for 85% recall. CodeGraph (colbymchenry/codegraph) shipped v0.8.0 on May 20 with answer-steering that delivers 35% cost and 70% token reduction across 7 real-world codebases. The rtk Rust CLI proxy (rtk-ai/rtk, 51.9k stars on May 21 snapshot) compresses shell command outputs before they reach LLM context, delivering 60–90% token reduction with zero dependencies. These are not prompt-engineering papers; each ships a reproducible benchmark or token log.

executive_summary.headline: Forge (antoinezambelli/forge) takes an 8B local model from 53% to 99% on multi-step agentic tasks using five domain-agnostic guardrail layers — accepted to ACM CAIS '26, 680 HN points
executive_summary.body: Show HN: Forge (May 19, 680 pts) is the week's highest-scored builder post. The thesis: a local 8B model with Forge guardrails (99.3%) outperforms Claude Sonnet without guardrails (87.2%). The guardrail stack is five layers — retry nudges, step enforcement, error recovery, rescue parsing, VRAM-aware context compaction — each independently toggleable. Error recovery scores 0% on every model tested, local and frontier, without the retry mechanism. That is an architectural absence, not a capability gap. The paper covers 97 model/backend configurations across 18 scenarios, 50 runs each. A proxy mode lets any OpenAI-compatible client route through Forge transparently.

executive_summary.headline: Datasette Agent ships first alpha — conversational SQL over any SQLite database with a plugin-first governance model that includes per-user USD spend caps
executive_summary.body: Simon Willison announced Datasette Agent on May 21 as the convergence of three years of LLM library work with Datasette. The architecture is plugin-first: the base agent handles conversational SQL queries, with datasette-agent-charts adding Observable Plot visualizations, datasette-agent-openai-imagegen adding image generation, and datasette-agent-sprites adding sandboxed code execution. Four alpha releases (0.1a1–0.1a4) shipped during the week. The datasette-llm-limits plugin (May 21) adds per-user USD spending caps — the governance primitive that enterprise teams need before wiring any LLM to internal data.

executive_summary.headline: Key takeaway: The open-source AI engineering community this week converged on one shared constraint — context cost — and attacked it from three independent angles: smarter retrieval (Semble, CodeGraph), compressed outputs (rtk), and reliability layers that prevent wasted retries (Forge).
executive_summary.body: Each of the three token-cost tools ships a different primitive: Semble replaces file-read cycles with semantic retrieval at the MCP layer; CodeGraph pre-indexes the codebase knowledge graph so agents navigate with fewer tool calls; rtk compresses shell output before it enters context. Together they address the three main token sources in a coding-agent session: retrieval, exploration, and command output. Forge adds the fourth dimension: reliability, which determines how many retries — and therefore how many wasted token cycles — a workflow generates. An enterprise AI team that treats these four as a stack rather than four independent experiments can materially reduce the per-task cost of agentic workflows on existing infrastructure.

top_picks.title: antoinezambelli/forge
top_picks.subtitle: Open-source reliability layer that takes an 8B local model from 53% to 99% on multi-step agentic workflows using five domain-agnostic guardrail layers — peer-reviewed at ACM CAIS '26
top_picks.author: antoinezambelli
top_picks.summary: Forge is an open-source reliability layer for self-hosted LLM tool-calling. Five independently toggleable guardrail layers wrap any local model. Result: Ministral 8B with Forge scores 99.3% on multi-step agentic benchmarks vs. 53% baseline; Claude Sonnet without guardrails scores 87.2%. Error recovery contributes 0% accuracy to every model tested without the retry mechanism. The paper covers 97 model/backend configurations, 18 scenarios, 50 runs each, accepted to ACM CAIS '26. A proxy mode routes any OpenAI-compatible client through Forge transparently.
key_takeaways: A local 8B model with Forge guardrails (99.3%) outperforms Claude Sonnet without guardrails (87.2%) — the reliability gap between frontier and local models is architectural, not capability-based.

Error recovery scores 0% for every model tested without the retry mechanism. Forge adds ToolResolutionError (distinguishing 'tool ran and found nothing' from 'tool ran and returned data'), which prevents bad data cascading downstream silently.

The same model weights score 7% vs. 83% depending on serving layer — a 75-point accuracy swing from infrastructure alone. Forge makes the serving configuration a first-class parameter in its eval harness.
top_picks.results: Ministral 8B with Forge: 99.3%. Claude Sonnet without Forge: 87.2%. 97 model/backend configurations, 18 scenarios, 50 runs each. Show HN: 680 pts (May 19, 2026). Paper: ACM CAIS '26, May 26–29, San Jose. Source: github.com/antoinezambelli/forge README and HN item 48192383.
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: Implementation pattern: Deploy Forge in proxy mode on an internal server and route your existing OpenAI-compatible agentic workflow clients through it — no application code changes required. Configure the retry nudge layer first (highest-impact layer: 24–49 point accuracy improvement in the paper's ablation study) and enable the VRAM-aware context manager to prevent silent CPU fallback on managed hardware. The step enforcement layer can encode your organization's required task sequencing (e.g., a read-before-write rule for database agents, or a plan-before-implement rule for coding agents) without any prompt engineering. | Regulated-environment caveats: Forge is Python-based and installs via pip; run a dependency audit before production deployment. The proxy mode intercepts all tool call traffic — ensure the Forge server is deployed within your network perimeter and logs are routed to your SIEM. The VRAM query via nvidia-smi at startup requires appropriate permissions on the host machine. Treat the backend configuration (serving layer, quant level, temperature) as part of the test fixture — small changes produce large accuracy swings per the paper. | 30-day experiment: Identify one internal multi-step agentic workflow that currently has a measurable failure rate. Deploy Forge in proxy mode with retry nudges and error recovery enabled. Run the workflow against a fixed test set of 20 inputs with and without Forge active. Compare completion rate, failure mode distribution, and token cost per successful completion.

top_picks.title: MinishLab/semble v0.2.0
top_picks.subtitle: Local MCP server for semantic code search — 98% fewer tokens than grep+read, indexes a repo in 250ms, queries in 1.5ms, CPU-only
top_picks.author: MinishLab
top_picks.summary: Semble is an MIT-licensed code search library and MCP server for AI coding agents. It replaces the grep+read cycle with local semantic retrieval using a 137M-parameter CPU-only model, achieving 98% fewer tokens and 94% recall at 2k tokens vs. 85% for grep+read at a 100k context window. v0.2.0 (May 21) adds non-blocking MCP server model loading. Average repo indexes in 250ms; queries resolve in 1.5ms. 218x faster indexing than CodeRankEmbed Hybrid, 10x faster queries, 99% of its retrieval quality. 3.6k stars.
key_takeaways: 98% fewer tokens at 94% recall vs. grep+read at 85% recall with a 100k context window — better retrieval quality at a fraction of the context cost.
Runs entirely on CPU with no external service dependencies, deployable inside a network perimeter without egress to any external model API.
218x indexing speed advantage over transformer-based alternatives means the index stays fresh without a background GPU process.
top_picks.results: 98% fewer tokens than grep+read. 94% recall at 2k tokens vs. 85% for grep+read at 100k. 218x faster indexing, 10x faster queries. 99% of CodeRankEmbed quality. Index time ~250ms. Query latency ~1.5ms. 3.6k GitHub stars. Show HN: 270 pts, 89 comments (May 18, 2026). Source: github.com/MinishLab/semble README.
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: Implementation pattern: Deploy Semble as an MCP server on developer workstations using the uvx one-command install. The server runs locally with no external API calls, safe for environments with controlled internet egress. Point approved coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor) at the Semble MCP endpoint and add the AGENTS.md snippet to project repositories. This replaces the grep+read cycle that inflates context windows on large monorepos. The token reduction is most pronounced on repositories with 10k+ files. | Regulated-environment caveats: The 137M-parameter model weights are downloaded on first use from a public model registry; host the approved checkpoint in your internal artifact registry after an initial dependency review. Semble indexes code locally — no code content leaves the host. Verify uvx installation is compatible with your managed endpoint security policies. | 30-day experiment: Pick a large internal codebase where coding agents currently use many sequential grep and cat tool calls. Install Semble as an MCP server on one developer's workstation and log token consumption per session with and without Semble active. Compare average tokens per successful task completion over 30 working days.

top_picks.title: colbymchenry/codegraph v0.8.0
top_picks.subtitle: Pre-indexed semantic code knowledge graph — v0.8.0 (May 20) cuts token cost 35% and tool calls 70% across 7 real-world codebases
top_picks.author: colbymchenry
top_picks.summary: CodeGraph is a TypeScript-based local SQLite code knowledge graph for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. v0.8.0 (May 20) adds answer-steering that delivers 35% cost reduction, 59% fewer tokens, 49% faster response, and 70% fewer tool calls vs. a no-graph baseline. Benchmarks run on 7 real-world open-source codebases using Claude Opus 4.7 / Claude Code v2.1.145. Excalidraw: 83→12 tool calls; Tokio: 75→9 tool calls. Supports 19+ languages, 100% local, no API keys. 12.9k stars, 741 forks.
key_takeaways: 70% tool-call reduction on complex codebases (Excalidraw: 83→12, Tokio: 75→9) directly reduces LLM inference cost — each tool call is a round trip to the model.
Benchmark methodology is reproducible: headless Claude Code with --strict-mcp-config, 4 runs per arm, median reported, against known public repos at --depth 1.
Framework-aware route detection (13 frameworks, 19+ languages) means the knowledge graph understands URL patterns and middleware chains, relevant for service-oriented codebases.
top_picks.results: 7 real-world codebases, 4 runs per arm, median reported. Average: 35% cheaper, 59% fewer tokens, 49% faster, 70% fewer tool calls. Best-case: Excalidraw (83→12 tool calls, $1.02→$0.54). Tested with Claude Opus 4.7 / Claude Code v2.1.145. 12.9k GitHub stars. Source: github.com/colbymchenry/codegraph README benchmarks.
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: Implementation pattern: Install CodeGraph as an MCP server against internal monorepo or service repositories. The SQLite index stays on the developer's machine — no code leaves the host. Use the auto-sync file watcher for incremental indexing; native OS events mean no full rebuild on change. For large codebases spanning multiple services, run one CodeGraph instance per service boundary to keep query latency low and context focused. | Regulated-environment caveats: Requires tree-sitter and SQLite with WASM fallbacks; validate WASM sandbox is permitted under your endpoint security policy. Pin the npm package to a specific version in your internal registry. Framework route detection is available for 13 frameworks; for internal frameworks, use the symbol-lookup functionality as baseline. | 30-day experiment: Run one developer's coding agent sessions for two weeks with CodeGraph disabled (baseline) and two weeks with it enabled, logging total tokens consumed and wall-clock time per merged PR. Compare per-PR cost at your current API rate.

top_picks.title: simonwillison/datasette-agent
top_picks.subtitle: First alpha of Datasette Agent — extensible AI assistant for Datasette with per-user spend caps and plugin-gated capabilities
top_picks.author: simonwillison
top_picks.summary: Datasette Agent is a plugin-first AI assistant for Datasette that answers natural-language questions against any SQLite database. Four companion plugins shipped the same week: base SQL querying, datasette-agent-charts (Observable Plot), datasette-agent-openai-imagegen (ChatGPT Images 2.0), datasette-agent-sprites (Fly Sprites sandboxed code execution). The datasette-llm-limits plugin (May 21) adds per-user USD spending caps. Four alpha releases (0.1a1–0.1a4) shipped during the week. Live demo at agent.datasette.io runs on Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite.
key_takeaways: datasette-llm-limits ships a per-user USD spending cap as a first-class configuration option — the governance primitive that allows an enterprise team to deploy a user-accessible data querying tool without open-ended LLM spend exposure.
The plugin-first architecture means teams can audit and approve individual capabilities (SQL queries, charts, code execution) independently rather than accepting a monolithic agent feature set.

Running on open-weight models in LM Studio locally is documented as a one-liner uvx command, enabling conversational data querying against internal databases without sending query content to a cloud endpoint.
top_picks.results: Four plugin releases (0.1a1–0.1a4) in a single week. Three companion plugins shipped. datasette-llm-limits 0.1a1 adds per-user spending caps. Live demo at agent.datasette.io. Source: simonwillison.net/2026/May/21/datasette-agent/.
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: Implementation pattern: Deploy datasette-agent on an internal Datasette instance pointed at internal SQLite databases (operational metrics, product telemetry, ERP exports). Configure datasette-llm-limits with a per-user daily USD cap to bound LLM spend. Start with the base SQL-querying functionality before enabling charts or code execution plugins — the SQL layer alone provides significant value and has the narrowest attack surface. Use the open-weight model path (LM Studio + uvx) to keep query content on-premises for databases containing regulated data. | Regulated-environment caveats: The code execution plugin (datasette-agent-sprites) runs code in cloud-hosted Fly Sprites sandboxes; disable this for data that cannot leave your network perimeter. The image generation plugin sends requests to ChatGPT Images 2.0; disable similarly. The base SQL and chart plugins can run with on-premises LLMs. The project is early alpha (0.1a4 as of May 24); audit the dependency tree before internal production deployment. | 30-day experiment: Point datasette-agent at one internal analytics dataset your team currently queries via manual SQL or a BI tool. Enable only the base SQL plugin and datasette-llm-limits with a $1/user/day cap. Have five analysts use it for routine data queries for two weeks. Measure time per query task vs. previous workflow and capture any SQL accuracy failures.

top_picks.title: rtk-ai/rtk
top_picks.subtitle: Single Rust binary that compresses shell command outputs before they reach LLM context — 60–90% token reduction on common dev commands
top_picks.author: rtk-ai
top_picks.summary: rtk (Rust Token Killer) is a CLI proxy that intercepts command outputs — ls, cat, grep, git, npm test, cargo test, pytest, docker ps — and compresses them before they enter the LLM context window. A typical 30-minute Claude Code session drops from ~150,000 tokens to ~45,000 tokens (70% reduction). Single zero-dependency Rust binary installable with one command. Integrates with Claude Code via hooks. Works with Cursor, Gemini CLI, Codex, Copilot. 51.9k stars on May 21 GitHub trending snapshot.
key_takeaways: 90% token reduction on test command output (npm test, cargo test, pytest) is the highest-leverage intervention — test output is verbose by design; rtk shows only failures, which is what agents need.
A single Rust binary with zero dependencies means the attack surface for supply-chain review is minimal and tractable.
Hook-first mode applies automatically to every agent conversation and subagent without per-session configuration.
top_picks.results: ~150,000 tokens per session → ~45,000 tokens (70% reduction). pytest -90%, npm test -90%, git push -92%, grep -80%, ls/tree -80%. 51.9k GitHub stars (May 21 trending snapshot). Source: github.com/rtk-ai/rtk README.
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: Implementation pattern: Deploy rtk in hook-first mode on developer workstations running sanctioned coding agents. The hook integrates with Claude Code's settings.json and applies automatically to all sessions. For teams with a standardized coding agent setup, include rtk initialization in your developer environment provisioning script. Works with Cursor, Gemini CLI, Codex, and Copilot regardless of which coding agent is approved for a given team. | Regulated-environment caveats: rtk is a Rust binary available via GitHub Releases; host the approved binary in your internal artifact registry and pin the version in provisioning scripts. Review the compression heuristics for any output format your agents treat as structured data — rtk is designed for developer workflow outputs. The hook modifies ~/.claude/settings.json; validate this is compatible with your managed endpoint security profile. | 30-day experiment: Deploy rtk on five developer workstations in hook-first mode. Compare total LLM API spend for those five developers against a control group of five without rtk over 30 days. Normalize by number of agent sessions per developer. Report the per-session and per-PR token cost delta.

items.title: Token cost engineering is now a first-class discipline, distinct from model selection
items.summary: Three independent projects shipped this week targeting context window cost from different angles: retrieval (Semble: 98% fewer tokens), exploration (CodeGraph: 70% fewer tool calls), and output compression (rtk: 60–90% token reduction). This is a pattern shift: the conversation has moved from 'which model to use' to 'how to make current models cheaper per task.' The two questions are now separable.

items.title: Spend controls and capability gating are emerging as table-stakes features in agentic frameworks
items.summary: Two distinct projects this week shipped spend controls as default features: datasette-llm-limits (per-user USD cap, configurable rolling window) and TensorZero (spend tracking listed as a core gateway feature). Forge's proxy mode routes all LLM traffic through a single local endpoint where logging and interception are possible. An enterprise AI team should now treat absence of spend controls and audit logging as a disqualifying characteristic when evaluating any new agentic framework.

items.title: Agent skills are converging on a cross-platform open standard — the same SKILL.md works across six coding agents
items.summary: Three separate skills repos trended this week (mattpocock/skills, obra/superpowers, addyosmani/agent-skills) — all using the same SKILL.md format adopted by Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and GitHub Copilot. A skill written once installs without modification across these six tools. An enterprise AI team that invests in writing internal skills (for compliance checks, internal tooling integration, engineering standards) gets that investment automatically across any coding agent the team adopts.
